title: Angular Basics: Components, Signals and Services
summary: Build apps the Angular way: components and templates, signals, control flow, inputs and outputs, services with dependency injection, and a multi-file project.
objectives: Explain what Angular is and how an Angular app starts up
Write components with templates, interpolation and event binding
Store changing data in signals and derive values with computed
Use @if, @for and property binding to render data
Pass data down with inputs and send events up with outputs
Share state across components with services and dependency injection

lessons.title: Your first Angular component
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Meet Angular **Angular** is a big toolkit for building apps, made by a team at Google. You write it in **TypeScript**, the JavaScript-with-labels you already know. Angular apps are built from **components**. A component is one piece of the page, like a badge, a menu or a game score. ### A component has two parts ```ts @Component({ selector: 'app-root', template: `

Hello, {{ name }}!

`, }) export class App { name = 'Pixel'; } ``` 1. The **class** at the bottom holds the data: `name = 'Pixel'`. 2. The **template** is the HTML the component shows. `@Component({ ... })` is a label on the class. It tells Angular "this class is a component". The `selector` is the tag where it goes. Here that's `` in **index.html**. ### Double curly braces `{{ name }}` means "put the value of `name` here". Angular swaps it for **Pixel** on the page. If you change `name`, the page changes too. ### New words - **Angular**: a toolkit for building apps out of components. - **Component**: a piece of the page made of a class (the data) and a template (the HTML). - **Template**: the HTML a component shows. - **Selector**: the tag name where a component goes, like `app-root`. - **Interpolation**: showing a value in the template with `{{ }}`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A Space Club welcome card. The class has two properties, and the template shows both with `{{ }}`. (In a real project the component and the start-up code live in separate files. Here it's all in one page so you can see everything at once.)

lessons.title: Components, templates and bootstrapping
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Why Angular?

React is a **library**: it renders components, and you choose other libraries for routing, forms and data. **Angular** is a **framework**: one toolkit from Google with all of those built in, plus strong opinions about how an app is organized. Large teams like that every Angular app looks alike, which is why it's common in big companies and government systems.

Angular is written in **TypeScript**, so everything you learned about types applies here.

### A component

```ts
import { Component } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  templateUrl: './app.html',
  styleUrl: './app.css',
})
export class App {
  title = 'Game Night';
}
```

`@Component({ ... })` is a **decorator**: a function that attaches **metadata** (information about the class) to the class below it. Angular reads it to learn:

- `selector`: the custom tag the component renders into, like `<app-root>`.
- `templateUrl` / `template`: the HTML, either in its own file or inline in backticks.
- `styleUrl` / `styles`: CSS that applies **only to this component**.

### Templates and interpolation

In the template, `{{ expression }}` is **interpolation**: Angular evaluates the expression against the component instance and inserts the result as text. You can read properties (`{{ title }}`), call methods (`{{ total() }}`) and do simple maths, but not assignments.

### How an Angular project starts

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `index.html` | Contains one `<app-root>` tag and loads `main.ts` |
| `main.ts` | `bootstrapApplication(App)` starts Angular and renders `App` into `<app-root>` |
| `app.ts`, `app.html`, `app.css` | The root component: class, template and styles |

A project made with the **Angular CLI** (`ng new`) also has an `app.config.ts` for app-wide settings. Here, `main.ts` is already written for you.

One difference from a real project: `ng build` compiles templates **ahead of time** and checks them for mistakes. In Codegrove the template is compiled in the browser when the page runs, so template typos show up as Console errors rather than red squiggles.

### New words

- **Framework**: a complete toolkit that decides the structure of your app. You fill in the parts.
- **Decorator**: a function written with `@` above a class that attaches metadata to it.
- **Metadata**: information about something, like a component's selector and template.
- **Interpolation**: `{{ }}` in a template, which shows the value of an expression as text.
- **Bootstrapping**: starting the app by rendering the root component into the page.
- **CLI** (*Command-Line Interface*): a tool you run by typing commands, like `ng new` and `ng serve`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A weather card with a property, a method and a bit of maths in the template. The CLI would split this into `app.ts`, `app.html` and `app.css`. Here the template and styles are inline so the whole example fits on one page.

lessons.title: Signals and clicks
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Values that change

A **signal** is a box that holds a value. Angular keeps an eye on the box. When the value inside changes, Angular updates the page for you.

```ts
score = signal(0);
```

### Read, set and update

- **Read** it by calling it like a function: `score()`. In the template: `{{ score() }}`
- **Set** a new value: `this.score.set(10);`
- **Update** it from the old value: `this.score.update((n) => n + 1);`

`(n) => n + 1` means "take the old number, give back one more".

### Clicks

To run a method when a button is clicked, put the event name in round brackets:

```html
<button (click)="addPoint()">+1</button>
```

Round brackets mean "when this happens, do that".

### New words

- **Signal**: a box for a value that Angular watches, so the page updates when it changes.
- **Event**: something that happens on the page, like a click.
- **Event binding**: `(click)="..."`, which runs code when the event happens.
- **Method**: a function that belongs to a class, like `addPoint()`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A cookie jar. Each click calls `eat()`, which updates the signal, and Angular redraws the number straight away.

lessons.title: Signals, events and computed values
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## State with signals

**State** is data that changes while the app runs: a score, a cart, whether a menu is open. In modern Angular, state lives in **signals**.

```ts
import { signal } from '@angular/core';

count = signal(0);          // a WritableSignal<number>

this.count();               // read: 0
this.count.set(5);          // replace the value
this.count.update((n) => n + 1);  // new value from the old one
```

A signal is a **reactive** value: when you read `count()` inside a template, Angular records that the template depends on it. When the value changes, Angular re-renders exactly the parts that read it. This lets Angular skip checking the whole page after every click. The older approach, a library called **zone.js**, did check everything; Angular 21 and later run **zoneless** by default.

### Derived values: computed

```ts
price = signal(4);
quantity = signal(3);
total = computed(() => this.price() * this.quantity());
```

A **computed signal** is read-only and recalculates when a signal it reads changes. Use it for anything you could work out from other state, instead of keeping a second copy in sync by hand.

### Event binding

```html
<button (click)="add()">Add</button>
<input (input)="search.set($any($event.target).value)" />
```

`(event)="statement"` runs the statement when the DOM event fires. `$event` is the event object. (`$any(...)` tells the template checker not to worry about the target's type.)

### The gotcha: update immutably

Angular compares a signal's old and new value with `===`. If you `push` into an array that's already in a signal, it's still the same array, so nothing re-renders. Always set a **new** array or object:

```ts
items.update((list) => [...list, 'new item']);   // ✓ new array
```

### New words

- **State**: data that changes while the app is running.
- **Signal**: a reactive value. Read it by calling it; change it with `set` or `update`.
- **Reactive**: automatically updating when the data it depends on changes.
- **Computed signal**: a read-only signal derived from other signals.
- **Event binding**: `(event)="..."` in a template, which runs code when a DOM event fires.
- **DOM** (*Document Object Model*): the browser's live tree of elements on the page.
- **Zoneless**: Angular's mode where signals, not zone.js, tell it when to re-render.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A tip calculator. `bill` and `tipPercent` are writable signals, `tip` and `total` are computed from them, and each button updates one signal. Notice there's no code that says "now redraw the total": the computed signals take care of it.

lessons.title: Control flow and property binding
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Built-in control flow Angular templates have **control flow blocks** for conditions and loops. They start with `@`. ```html @if (user(); as u) {

Welcome back, {{ u.name }}

} @else if (loading()) {

Loading…

} @else { Sign in } ``` ```html @for (task of tasks(); track task.id) {
  • {{ $index + 1 }}. {{ task.title }}
    • } @empty {
  • Nothing to do!
    • } ``` - `track` is **required**. It gives each item an identity, so when the list changes Angular can move, add or remove just the matching DOM elements instead of rebuilding the whole list. Track by a unique id when you have one. Use `$index` only for lists that never reorder. - Inside the loop you also get `$index`, `$count`, `$first`, `$last`, `$even` and `$odd`. - `@empty` renders when the list has no items. - `@switch (value) { @case ('a') { … } @default { … } }` picks one of several branches. (Older code uses `*ngIf` and `*ngFor` **directives** instead. You'll still meet them in existing projects; the blocks replaced them in Angular 17.) ### Property binding Square brackets bind a DOM **property** to an expression: ```html ``` Without brackets, `disabled="false"` would be the plain *text* "false", and the button would still be disabled. With brackets, the value is the expression's result. Two shortcuts: ```html
  • …
    • ``` ### The binding cheat sheet | Syntax | Direction | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | `{{ }}` | data → text | `{{ name() }}` | | `[prop]` | data → property | `[disabled]="busy()"` | | `(event)` | event → code | `(click)="save()"` | ### New words - **Control flow block**: `@if`, `@for`, `@switch` and friends, which decide what a template renders. - **Track expression**: the `track` part of `@for`, which gives every item an identity. - **Property binding**: `[property]="expression"`, which sets a DOM property from data. - **Class binding**: `[class.name]="condition"`, which adds the class only while the condition is true. - **Directive**: a class that adds behaviour to an element. `*ngIf` and `*ngFor` are the older directive versions of `@if` and `@for`.

lessons.title: Component inputs and outputs
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Data down, events up

Angular apps are a **component tree**: `App` at the root, children inside it, their children inside them. Information flows in two directions:

- **Inputs** carry data **down** from parent to child.
- **Outputs** carry events **up** from child to parent.

The child never reaches into its parent. It announces "something happened", and the parent decides what to do. That keeps children reusable.

### Inputs

```ts
export class Avatar {
  name = input.required<string>();   // parent must pass it
  size = input(48);                  // optional, defaults to 48 (type: number)
}
```

```html
<app-avatar name="Sam" />              <!-- a plain string -->
<app-avatar [name]="user().name" [size]="96" />   <!-- an expression -->
```

Inputs are **read-only signals** inside the child: call `name()` to read it. Without square brackets, the value is the literal text. With them, it's an expression.

### Outputs

```ts
export class LikeButton {
  liked = output<number>();      // will send a number
  click() { this.liked.emit(42); }
}
```

```html
<app-like-button (liked)="onLiked($event)" />
```

`$event` in the parent is whatever the child passed to `emit`.

### Using a component

A standalone component lists what its template uses in `imports: [Avatar, LikeButton]`. If you forget, Angular reports **NG0303: Can't bind to 'name' since it isn't a known property of 'app-avatar'**. That message almost always means a missing import.

(`model()` combines both: a writable input with a matching output, for two-way binding with `[(value)]`. Older code uses `@Input()` and `@Output()` decorators instead of these functions.)

### New words

- **Component tree**: the nesting of components, with the root component at the top.
- **Input**: a value a parent passes down into a child, made with `input()` or `input.required<T>()`.
- **Output**: an event a child sends up to its parent, made with `output<T>()` and sent with `emit`.
- **Emit**: send an output's event, with a value, to whoever is listening.
- **Standalone component**: a component that lists its own dependencies in `imports` (the default since Angular 19).
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A star rating component with a required input and an output. The parent passes `max` down and listens for `rated` coming back up. The child doesn't know or care what the parent does with the rating.

lessons.title: Project: Pet Shelter app
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Put it all together

Time to build a real little app! You'll use everything from this course:

- a **component** with a template
- a **signal** that holds a list
- **@for** to repeat a card for every pet
- an **input** to pass each pet's name into its card
- a **service** that keeps the list of pets
- a **click** that adds a new pet

### One new trick: naming a text box

Put `#` and a name on a tag, and the template can use that name:

```html
<input #nickname />
<button (click)="greet(nickname.value)">Say hi</button>
```

`#nickname` is a **template reference**. `nickname.value` is whatever is typed in the box.

### Passing an input from a loop

To give each card a different name, use square brackets:

```html
@for (pet of pets(); track $index) {
  <app-pet-card [name]="pet" />
}
```

Square brackets mean "use the value of `pet`", not the word "pet".

### New words

- **Template reference**: a `#name` on a tag, so the template can use that element.
- **Property binding**: `[name]="pet"`, which passes a value instead of plain text.
- **App**: a program made of components that work together.

lessons.title: Project: Quest Board
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## A small, real Angular app

This project is laid out the way an Angular team would build it:

| File | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `quest.ts` | The `Quest` **model**: an interface describing one quest |
| `quest.service.ts` | All the state and rules: add, toggle, count what's left |
| `quest-item.ts` | A **presentational** component: shows one quest, emits `toggled` |
| `app.ts`, `app.html`, `app.css` | The **container**: injects the service and wires everything together |

**Presentational** components only take inputs and emit outputs, so they're easy to reuse and test. **Container** components know about services. Splitting them this way is a common Angular habit.

### Immutable updates with map and filter

Signals notice a change when the value is a new object. To change one item in a list, build a new list:

```ts
this.list.update((all) =>
  all.map((q) => (q.id === id ? { ...q, done: !q.done } : q)),
);
```

`map` returns a new array; the spread `{ ...q, done: … }` makes a new object for the one quest that changed and reuses the others. Counting works the same way: `filter` returns a new array of matching items, and `.length` counts them.

### Forms and template references

```html
<form (submit)="$event.preventDefault(); addQuest(newQuest)">
  <input #newQuest />
</form>
```

`#newQuest` is a **template reference variable**: it points at the input element itself, so the component method receives an `HTMLInputElement`. Pressing Enter or clicking the button submits the form; `preventDefault()` stops the browser from reloading the page. (For bigger forms, Angular has **reactive forms** in `@angular/forms`, with validation built in.)

### New words

- **Model**: a type that describes the app's data, like `Quest`.
- **Presentational component**: a component that only uses inputs and outputs, with no services.
- **Container component**: a component that injects services and passes data to presentational children.
- **Immutable update**: changing data by making a new copy instead of editing the original.
- **Template reference variable**: `#name` on an element, giving the template a reference to it.

hints.markdown: Signals only notice a new value. In `toggle`, how can you get a new array where just one quest has changed?
hints.speechText: Signals only notice a new value. In toggle, how can you get a new array where just one quest has changed?

hints.markdown: `add`: `const clean = title.trim(); if (!clean) return;` then `update` with `[...all, { id: this.nextId++, title: clean, done: false }]`. `toggle`: `all.map((q) => (q.id === id ? { ...q, done: !q.done } : q))`. `remaining`: `computed` over `filter((q) => !q.done).length`.
hints.speechText: In add, trim the title and return early if it's empty, then append a new quest object. In toggle, map over the list and replace only the matching quest with a copy where done is flipped. Remaining is a computed signal that filters out done quests and takes the length.

hints.markdown: In app.html: `@for (quest of quests.quests(); track quest.id) { <app-quest-item [quest]="quest" (toggled)="quests.toggle($event)" /> } @empty { … }`
hints.speechText: In the template, loop over quests dot quests, tracking quest dot id. Render a quest item, bind its quest input, and send its toggled event to quests dot toggle. Then add the empty block.

questions.prompt: Why does toggle use map instead of changing q.done directly?
questions.explanation: Signals compare old and new values; a new array (and a new object for the changed quest) is a visible change.

options.text: So the signal gets a new array and Angular sees the change
Because map is faster than a loop
Because done is read-only in TypeScript
